title: Building a banking regime for the future - speech by David Bailey
summary: David Bailey of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) outlined the Bank of England's current pipeline of reforms related to banking sector capital and liquidity at a JPM UK Banks ALM Conference on 28 April 2026. The speech emphasized that the PRA is shifting from a decade of post-crisis resilience building to now focusing on efficiency, proportionality, and modernization of the prudential framework. Key initiatives include Basel 3.1 implementation (with January 2026 publication, firms must be ready by the start of 2027), the Strong and Simple regime, and the ongoing ring-fencing regime. Bailey emphasized balancing resilience with competitiveness and growth objectives while maintaining the UK's position as a major global financial centre.
key_points: The PRA requires banks to hold capital for three reasons: to absorb unexpected losses, to support customers through downturns, and to enable orderly failure without taxpayer costs
The UK banking system is approximately 20x leveraged, making it inherently vulnerable to confidence shocks and maturity mismatches
Basel 3.1 standards were published in January 2026, with firms required to be ready by the start of 2027
The ring-fencing regime structurally separates core retail banking from wholesale and investment activities to prevent shocks in one part of a group destabilizing essential retail services

The PRA's secondary objective (competitiveness and growth) came into effect in 2023, pushing the authority to understand how regulation influences growth through three foundations: maintaining trust, operating efficiently, and being responsive to innovation
The current regulatory focus has shifted from resilience building to efficiency, proportionality, and ensuring the framework evolves with the financial system
Key areas of reform include the Strong and Simple regime, Basel 3.1 implementation, and examining whether parts of the regime have become overly complex or could be better targeted
why_it_matters: This speech signals the PRA's regulatory direction for UK banks over the next several years. Market participants need to understand that the era of tightening capital and liquidity requirements is giving way to a more nuanced approach focused on efficiency and proportionality. For bank equities, this could be incrementally positive as regulatory burden discussions shift tone. For fixed income investors in bank capital instruments (AT1, Tier 2), the speech reinforces that resilience standards remain high even as the focus shifts to calibration. The timing is notable—firms have until the start of 2027 to implement Basel 3.1, making this a critical compliance milestone.
market_structure_context: The speech directly addresses the structure of the UK banking system: the regulatory framework governing capital (CET1, AT1, Tier 2), liquidity requirements (LCR, NSFR), the ring-fencing architecture separating retail and wholesale banking, and the balance between resilience and efficiency in prudential regulation. Bailey explicitly connected regulatory structure to financial stability, noting that the UK system's 20x leverage makes it vulnerable to confidence shocks, which is why the framework requires banks to hold capital and liquidity buffers. The ring-fencing regime fundamentally reshaped how banking groups are structured by separating essential retail services from riskier wholesale activities.
